summary: Updates RFC 4458 by adding a predefined value for the SIP cause URI parameter for service number translation retargeting.

plainLanguage.summary: A call note gets a new reason code: the number was changed to a real one.

questions: what is the sip cause uri parameter
how does history-info work with cause
subtitle: A new SIP 'cause' value, 380, records that a call was redirected because a service number was translated.

tldr.problem: Phone services such as toll-free numbers translate a dialed service access number into a routable one, and the receiving side loses track of which number the caller originally dialed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds the value 380, 'Service number translation', to the SIP 'cause' URI parameter and explains how to carry it in the History-Info header field so the original number can be found.
tldr.outcome: A user agent can recover the requested service number, provided the History-Info header field survives along the path. The procedures are meant for networks that use 3GPP-defined services.

today: RFC 8119 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 4458; it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. The text says its procedures are intended for networks that use 3GPP-defined services.

sections.title: The Problem: Service Number Translation
sections.content:
RFC 4458 defined a cause URI parameter that tells a SIP user agent server (UAS) why a request reached it. Its values mirror the redirecting reasons of the old telephone network, such as call forwarding.

The telephone network has another kind of retargeting. Intelligent Network services (Freephone, Virtual Private Network, Universal Personal Telecommunication) translate a service access number, a dialable number that is not globally routable, into a routable SIP or tel URI. ISUP keeps the original in its 'called IN number' and 'original called IN number' parameters. This RFC lets SIP interwork with them.

The text says the procedures are intended for networks that use 3GPP-defined services, and their use is undefined for other networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A special number like a toll-free line is like a nickname. The phone system swaps it for the real address, and this RFC makes sure the nickname is not forgotten.

sections.title: The New Cause Value
sections.content:
The RFC defines one new predefined value for the cause parameter of sip: and sips: URIs: 380, meaning 'Service number translation'. It may appear in the Request-URI and in the History-Info header field when the URI results from a service that translates an access number and is not a call forwarding service.

The grammar stays as in RFC 4458: cause-param = "cause=" Status-Code, with a companion target-param = "target=" pvalue. As in RFC 4458, the service must encode the cause parameter in the new target URI.
sections.plainLanguage: It is one new reason code on the list, number 380, that means 'we changed the number for a service'.

sections.title: Guidelines for Using the Parameter
sections.content:
The RFC fills a gap in RFC 4458 by explaining how cause works with the History-Info header field of RFC 7044. When a proxy puts a URI with cause into the Request-URI, it must also copy that URI into a History-Info entry. Then the information survives even if a downstream proxy replaces the Request-URI.

At the application server: when it turns a service access number into a routable one, it should add cause=380 to the new Request-URI and add a History-Info entry. It may also add a target parameter holding the Request-URI it received.

At the UAS: to learn which service number was dialed, it should look for cause value 380 in History-Info. That entry should carry an mp or rc parameter pointing to the entry with the matching index, which holds the requested number. Without it, the UAS can use the preceding entry.

The cause URI parameter is not the cause parameter of the Reason header field in RFC 3326. The Reason one should be added to a History-Info entry only when retargeting is due to a received SIP response.
sections.plainLanguage: Every stop the call makes writes down what happened, like a travel diary. The person who answers reads the diary to find the number you first dialed.

sections.title: When History-Info Is Missing
sections.content:
If History-Info is not supported or a proxy removed it, the original number may be lost. The RFC strongly recommends supporting History-Info all along the signaling path.

Without it, there is no guarantee. If the UAS is the direct target of the application and the Request-URI has cause=380, the number may be in the target parameter. If neither exists, the UAS cannot reliably find the number. Some implementations read the To header field, but that works only in some situations because intermediaries sometimes change it undetectably.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone tears pages out of the travel diary, you may not find the first number. Keeping the diary safe is the best fix.

sections.title: Example: A Toll-Free Call to a Call Center
sections.content:
Alice calls her bank's customer care line. John works in a call center that handles several toll-free services, and he needs to know which one Alice dialed so he can use the right welcome speech.

The INVITE first reaches the toll-free service with +18005551002 in the Request-URI. The service translates it to +15555551002@atlanta.com, adds cause=380, and builds a History-Info header with two entries. The second has index=1.1;mp=1. The call center proxy then routes to John and adds a third entry with index=1.1.1;rc=1.1. John can find the dialed toll-free number in the first entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice dials the bank's toll-free number. The system swaps it for John's desk and writes down the first number, so John knows which greeting to use.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA modified the existing cause row in the 'SIP/SIPS URI Parameters' subregistry to reference both RFC 4458 and this document.

The security considerations of RFC 4458 apply. If a privacy level of header is requested in the Privacy header field (RFC 3323), the cause parameter must be removed from the Request-URI. Privacy of parameters inside History-Info is covered by RFC 7044.
sections.plainLanguage: If a caller asks for privacy, the note about the swapped number has to be scratched out before the call moves on.

messages.label: INVITE F1
messages.note: Request-URI holds the dialed toll-free number.

messages.label: INVITE F2
